review.review_summary: 10 claims checked against the evidence; 4 flagged (1 unsupported, 2 overstated).
gaps: The evidence shows Support has the lowest mean salary ($62,996) but does not explain whether this reflects job-level mix, experience, or market rates. Comparing Support salaries to other departments within the same job levels would clarify whether the gap is structural.

The claim about attrition trends ('highest in four years') requires historical attrition rates by period, but the evidence provides only the 12-month attrition rate to 31 Oct 2026 (29.6%). A trend analysis across prior years is not shown.

The evidence does not show which employees are 'flight risks' or how they were identified. Claim 7 names 10 Support employees for retention plans, but no evidence item lists individuals or flags them as at-risk.
next_investigations: Compare mean annual salary in Support to other departments within each job level to determine whether the $62,996 average reflects lower-level roles or a true pay gap at equivalent levels.

Analyze attrition rate by department and termination category (voluntary vs. involuntary) over the 12-month period to identify whether Support's attrition is primarily voluntary and whether it differs from other departments.
methodology_concerns: Attrition is defined as separations ÷ average month-end headcount over 12 months, but the evidence does not show the month-end headcount figures used in the denominator or break down separations by voluntary vs. involuntary within departments. This limits the ability to assess whether Support's attrition is driven by voluntary departures or other factors.

claims.text: Low pay is driving attrition: Support, the lowest-paid department, loses the most people, so raising Support salaries would cut its attrition.
As of 31 Oct 2026, the organisation employs 885 people (839.0 FTE), with 286 separations recorded over the prior 12 months driving a 29.6% attrition rate — 15.9% of which was voluntary.
Pay spread across departments and a high attrition rate are the two areas most deserving immediate attention.
Attrition so far in 2026 is 26.2%, an annual attrition rate of 31.4% if the pace holds, the highest in four years.
Only 2 women in Legal left this year, both from the same team.
The overall annual salary distribution is wide — from $19,100 to $217,100 — with a median of $69,300 and a mean of $76,006, and outliers have been flagged but kept in the data.

The dataset covers hire dates from 2015 to 2026 across 885 employees recorded in 1,770 rows, meaning each employee appears more than once (e.g. across role or status changes), so headcount should never be read from row counts.
Ten Support employees are flight risks and should be put on retention plans now. Reducing voluntary attrition would directly lower replacement costs and preserve institutional knowledge.

Review the pay gap between Support ($62,996 average) and the organisation-wide median ($69,300) to assess whether compensation is competitive enough to retain staff in that department. Support is the lowest-paid department and may be contributing disproportionately to attrition.

Examine the high-salary outliers (up to $217,100) to confirm they are correctly classified and not data errors before using salary figures in any pay-equity or benchmarking work. Outliers inflate the mean and could distort department-level comparisons.

Read as HR data (headcount, FTE, separations, attrition rate, voluntary attrition, hires, average salary (current staff)). Headcount is the people in force at the latest date (contractors and agency workers out, interns and part-timers in); separations and hires are events (a rehire's exits count separately); attrition is separations ÷ the average of the month-end headcounts over the 12 months to that date. Pay and protected attributes (gender, ethnicity) are never shown for groups of fewer than 11 people.
Gender is shown as a description only: hiring, firing or pay decisions on it are discrimination, so no recommendation is made on it; groups of fewer than 11 people are not shown.
Ethnicity is special-category data (GDPR Art. 9): shown as a description only, never a recommendation about people, and never for groups of fewer than 11.
Performance ratings describe groups here; they are never used to rank or predict individuals.

review.review_summary: 8 claims checked against the evidence; 2 flagged (1 unsupported, 1 contradicted).
gaps: The report does not show attrition by department or tenure, which the user's question asks for in claim 6 (an action). Breakdown of the 49 separations by department and employee tenure would be needed to identify where retention efforts should focus.

No evidence on the composition of the 70 hires (by department, worker type, or hire date) is shown. Understanding where new joiners were placed would help assess whether they contributed disproportionately to separations.
The report does not show headcount or FTE trends over the 24-month period. Month-by-month or quarter-by-quarter headcount would reveal whether attrition and hiring patterns are stable or changing.
next_investigations: Break down the 49 separations by department and compare to headcount by department as of 31 Oct 2026 to identify which departments have the highest attrition rates.
Segment separations by tenure (months between hire date and termination date) to determine whether recent hires account for a disproportionate share of the 49 separations.
Compare average base salary by department and worker type to assess whether pay differences correlate with attrition or hiring patterns.
methodology_concerns: Attrition is calculated as separations ÷ average month-end headcount over 12 months. The evidence does not show the month-end headcounts used in the denominator, so the 14.3% figure cannot be independently verified from the data shown.

claims.text: As of 31 Oct 2026, the workforce stands at 353 employees with an annual attrition rate of 14.3% and a median base salary of $82,700.
The dataset covers 24 months of monthly HR snapshots (Nov 2024 – Oct 2026) across 8,220 employees, tracking headcount, pay, hires, and separations.
Hiring 70 people in 12 months is what pushed attrition up to 14.3%: the new joiners left first.
The workforce totals 353 employees (338.40 FTE) as of 31 Oct 2026, with 70 hires and 49 separations over the prior 12 months, yielding an attrition rate of 14.3%.
Base salary ranges widely — from $34,400 to $170,800 — with a median of $82,700 and a mean of $84,622; salary outliers have been flagged but kept in the data.
Average base salary is broadly similar across the six departments, with Marketing averaging $87,825 and Finance the lowest at $83,437.

Investigate the drivers of the 14.3% attrition rate by department and tenure to identify where retention efforts should be focused. 49 separations in 12 months represent meaningful workforce disruption and replacement cost.

Review the salary outliers flagged in base salary to confirm they reflect legitimate roles rather than data errors before using pay data in decisions. The $34,400–$170,800 range is wide; unverified outliers could distort any pay equity or benchmarking analysis.
